common_name: Avoyelles Sweet Potato (Early-Maturing LSU AgCenter 2024 Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; released by the LSU AgCenter in June 2024, named for the Avoyelles Parish sweet potato industry, and matures in as little as 90 days, notably earlier than the 110-120 days typical of many commercial varieties.

directions: Avoyelles has light rose-to-copper, mostly smooth skin over uniformly deep orange flesh that bakes to a bright color, and was bred for southern root-knot nematode resistance. It was the top-ranked variety for total and U.S. No. 1 yield across LSU AgCenter multi-state trials leading up to its release. Its early 90-day maturity makes it a good fit for Gulf Coast gardeners who want to free up bed space sooner than Beauregard or Covington allow. As the first new LSU sweet potato variety released in over a decade, it represents the current state of the breeding program's disease-resistance work.
sources: LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station

common_name: Burgundy Sweet Potato (LA 04-175, Disease-Resistant Red-Skin LSU Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; breeding line LA 04-175, matures equal to or slightly earlier than Beauregard and was released by the LSU AgCenter with strong multi-disease resistance.

directions: Burgundy is a red-skinned, orange-fleshed, high-yielding sweet potato developed by the LSU AgCenter, valued for resistance to Streptomyces soil rot, Fusarium wilt (stem rot), and southern root-knot nematode. It matures on roughly the same schedule as Beauregard, making it a straightforward substitute for growers wanting improved disease tolerance without a longer season. Flesh color and eating quality are similar to other standard orange-fleshed Louisiana releases, cooking moist and sweet after curing. Its multi-pathogen resistance package is particularly useful in Gulf Coast gardens with a history of nematode or soil rot pressure.
sources: LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station

common_name: Excel Sweet Potato (High-Yield NCSU Copper-Skin Orange Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a North Carolina State University release bred for high yield and broad disease resistance, useful where nematodes, stem rot, or internal cork have been problems for other varieties.

directions: Excel has light copper skin over orange flesh and is noted for out-yielding Jewel by roughly 15% in North Carolina State University trials. It carries strong resistance to southern root-knot nematode, stem rot (Fusarium wilt), and internal cork, making it a dependable choice for gardens with a history of these problems. Baking and canning quality are considered excellent, and roots store well after curing. Flavor and texture are comparable to other classic moist, orange-fleshed dessert-type sweet potatoes.

common_name: Heartogold Sweet Potato (1947 LSU Heirloom, Tan Skin Bright Orange Flesh)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; developed by LSU AgCenter breeder Julian C. Miller and released in 1947. Young transplants look spindly at first but grow vigorously once established.

directions: Heartogold is an early, heavy-yielding heirloom bred by Julian C. Miller at the LSU Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1947, producing tan-skinned roots with bright orange flesh on vigorous vining plants. It is one of the older Louisiana-bred varieties still maintained in germplasm collections, predating the Jewel-Beauregard-Covington succession of commercial standards. Sclerotial blight, a soil-borne fungal disease, tends to show up on Heartogold more readily than on many other varieties, so avoid planting in poorly drained or previously infected beds. Cure roots at warm temperature and high humidity after harvest to develop full sweetness before storage.
sources: LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station

common_name: Beniazuma Sweet Potato (Classic Japanese Purplish-Red-Skin, Yellow-Flesh Satsumaimo)

planting.note: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a classic Japanese satsumaimo cultivar first developed in Ibaraki Prefecture in the 1980s and needs the full warm season to size up.

directions: Beniazuma is a Japanese satsumaimo (sweet potato) cultivar first produced in Ibaraki Prefecture in the 1980s, with purplish-red skin, firm yellow flesh, and a drier, flakier texture than typical American orange-fleshed types. Its mild sweetness and dense texture make it well suited to Japanese preparations such as yaki-imo (stone- or oven-roasted sweet potato), tempura, and sweet potato desserts. It remains widely grown in Japan's Kanto region, though acreage there has been overtaken in recent years by the sweeter Beniharuka. Curing after harvest improves both sweetness and storage life.

common_name: Beniharuka Sweet Potato (Japan's Top-Grown Ultra-Sweet Purple-Skin Satsumaimo)

planting.note: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; registered in March 2010 by Japan's Kyushu Okinawa Agricultural Research Center and became the most widely grown sweet potato variety in Japan by 2022.

directions: Beniharuka was bred from a cross of Beniazuma and Kyushu No. 30 in the early 1990s and registered as a cultivar in March 2010 by Japan's Kyushu Okinawa Agricultural Research Center. It has reddish-purple skin and pale yellow flesh that turns almost melt-in-the-mouth soft and intensely sweet when baked, and by 2022 it had become the top-acreage sweet potato variety in Japan, prized by growers for high yield and by consumers for its rich sweetness and moist, sticky texture after curing and long storage. It is popular for yaki-imo roasted sweet potatoes and other dessert-style preparations. Curing and extended storage continue to raise its sugar content, so it benefits from patience after harvest.

common_name: Red Japanese Sweet Potato (Reddish-Purple Skin, Dry White-Flesh Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; matures in about 95 days, a relatively short season for a dry-fleshed type, and is offered as slips by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange.

directions: Red Japanese produces deep reddish-purple skin over creamy white flesh, with a drier, denser texture than common moist orange varieties and a sweet, nutty flavor suited to roasting, steaming, frying, and baking. It is a vigorous, disease-resistant vine that reaches maturity in about 95 days, a shorter season than many dry-fleshed sweet potatoes require. Its adaptability to a range of summer climates has made it a long-standing offering among heirloom seed exchanges. Cure roots at warm temperature and high humidity after digging to firm the skin and develop full flavor.

common_name: Southern Queen Sweet Potato (19th-Century White-Skin White-Flesh Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a dependable 19th-century heirloom, introduced from South America around 1870, that matures in roughly 105 days.

directions: Southern Queen is a vining 19th-century heirloom, introduced into the United States from South America around 1870, that produces long, narrow tubers with white skin and white, dry-cooking flesh. Sometimes called the White Yam, it is one of the oldest sweet potato varieties still maintained in American cultivation, alongside Nansemond and Hayman. Its dry, starchy texture and mild flavor make it well suited to traditional Southern cooking styles that favor a less-sweet, more potato-like sweet potato. It matures in roughly 100-110 days and adapts to a wide range of growing conditions.

common_name: Murasaki-29 Sweet Potato (Nematode-Resistant Purple-Skin White-Flesh LSU Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a distinct Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station release bred from L89-72, separate from the older Japanese Murasaki cultivar already grown, and selected for root-knot nematode resistance.

directions: Murasaki-29 was bred by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station from an open-pollinated cross with the female parent L89-72 as a specialty white-flesh alternative to orange-fleshed dessert types like Beauregard. It has purple skin and white flesh, with shorter, elliptical, non-lobed storage roots compared to Beauregard. Unlike many other white-flesh specialty types such as O'Henry, Murasaki-29 carries useful resistance to southern root-knot nematode, comparable to Covington, Evangeline, and Jewel. Its firmer, less sweet flesh suits roasting and savory preparations rather than the moist, syrupy texture of orange-fleshed baking types.

planting.note: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; grown in Southside Virginia since 1850 and is one of the oldest sweet potato heirlooms still in cultivation.

directions: Nansemond is a 19th-century heirloom named for Nansemond County in Southside Virginia, where it has been a favorite home-garden variety since 1850. It produces yellow-fleshed roots on vigorous vines, with a red-skinned subvariety also historically grown in the region. Regionally it has traditionally been baked into sweet potato pies, sometimes made with toasted peanuts or peanut flour worked into the crust. Along with Southern Queen and Hayman, it remains one of the dependable pre-1900 sweet potato varieties still maintained by heirloom seed preservationists.
